description: HealthCoders. Our team focuses on one challenge: How to make the astronauts stay healthy while he is in the space? Our team goal is to find a creative solution for this problem by creating a Monitoring System for the astronaut.
summary:
Track Your Health (TYH) is our response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge to develop health monitoring software for astronauts on long-duration missions. As humanity prepares for deep-space exploration, astronauts face the RIDGE risks: Radiation, Isolation, Distance from Earth, Gravity fields, and hostile Environments.

TYH is a visually immersive, client-side React application designed to help astronauts independently monitor their physical and mental health. Its features include an interactive "Living Body Twin" that visualizes health status, daily vital tracking, mental well-being check-ins, and dynamic health charts.

To address psychological challenges and communication delays, TYH offers a "Calm Zone" featuring guided breathing, simulated delayed messages from home, and NOVA, a rule-based AI coach. It also includes a "Mission Simulator" where astronauts practice responding to emergencies such as solar storms and medical crises, alongside an educational nutrition guide based on NASA and CSA data.

We chose this challenge because future space exploration requires astronauts to take a more active role in managing their own health. By combining health monitoring, psychological support, and interactive emergency training in one offline-capable platform, TYH aims to improve astronaut safety, preparedness, and performance during long-duration space missions.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?
Track Your Health (TYH) is an immersive, self-contained health monitoring and training web application for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It functions as a digital health companion. The app features a "Living Body Twin"—an interactive, animated SVG human body where astronauts can click on organs (like the heart, lungs, or brain) to see their current health status, related indicators, and spaceflight risks. Users input their daily vitals (heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood) into a Daily Check-in form. The app evaluates this data against NASA-informed thresholds, providing real-time Green/Yellow/Red assessments and actionable guidance. It also includes a time-pressured Mission Simulator to train for emergencies, a Calm Zone for mental health support, and a rule-based AI coach named NOVA that provides personalized tips.

What benefits does it have?
TYH bridges the critical gap in autonomous deep-space healthcare. By shifting health management from Earth-based flight surgeons to the crew, it directly addresses the communication delays of missions to Mars. It provides a unified platform that tracks physical health, mitigates psychological isolation, and trains astronauts to make life-saving decisions under pressure. Furthermore, it is fully client-side, ensuring zero-latency performance and privacy without requiring continuous internet connectivity.

What is the intended impact of the project?
The intended impact is to ensure the safety, performance, and mental well-being of astronauts embarking on humanity's most ambitious journeys to the Moon and Mars. By gamifying health tracking and emergency training, TYH builds a culture of proactive health management. Beyond space, the app's educational content on nutrition, radiation, and isolation serves as a powerful tool to inspire students and the public about the realities of human spaceflight.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML, CSS.
  • Frontend: React, TanStack Router (for seamless SPA navigation), Tailwind CSS (for a responsive, space-themed UI), Recharts (for dynamic radar/trend charts), and Lucide (for iconography).
  • Deployment: GitHub for version control and Vercel for static hosting.

How is your project creative?
Our creativity lies in transforming dry medical data into an engaging, interactive experience. The "Living Body Twin" uses SVG animations to make the human body feel "alive"—the heart pulses at the astronaut's real-time heart rate, and lungs breathe. The Mission Simulator is a unique addition; it creates a cinematic, high-pressure environment with screen shakes and countdown timers to train astronauts for sudden solar storms or medical crises. Furthermore, the Calm Zone creatively tackles isolation by simulating delayed "Home Link" messages from Earth, giving astronauts a psychological lifeline.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Scientific Accuracy: We relied strictly on NASA’s "RIDGE" hazard framework and CSA research (e.g., lunar dust impacts, radiation limits) to ensure educational content is factual.
  • User Experience (UX): We designed the UI to be high-contrast, dark-mode, and large enough for tap targets, considering the stress and physical constraints astronauts face.
  • Technical Constraints: We prioritized a lightweight, fully client-side architecture to ensure the app functions flawlessly in deep space where internet connectivity is non-existent.
  • Accessibility: The app includes a help section for beginners, ensuring that users (even those without a medical background) can understand their health data.
